new_statements.quote: All present-day Bungku-Tolaki languages are open syllable languages, with the only syllable patterns being V and CV. Most roots are disyllabic, though occasionally three and four syllable roots are found. Stress is penultimate (non-phonemic), with suffixation usually precipitating stress movement.

new_statements.relation_note: Family-wide statement covering Rahambuu (a Bungku-Tolaki language); matches the catalog penultimate stress (penultimate). No Rahambuu-specific example.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress falls on the penultimate syllable in all present-day Bungku-Tolaki languages (Rahambuu included); it is non-phonemic and shifts rightward under suffixation to stay penultimate.
new_statements.exceptions: None for placement; footnote 4 argues that phonetically long vowels reported for Moronene are sequences of two like vowels 'as may be argued from patterns of stress placement' (i.e. stress placement treats VV as two syllables).
new_statements.identity_note: Both held statements are family-level (Bungku-Tolaki) generalisations that explicitly include Rahambuu as a member; neither gives a Rahambuu-specific stress example. Mead 2024 is a Sulawesi-wide historical overview (Glottolog's Glottolog's most extensive description pointer for Rahambuu is its p. 154) and, if opened, would at best restate the family-level penultimate rule.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word lists (Rahambuu among them) are written without stress marks because stress is predictably on the penultimate written vowel; long vowels are two like vowels, so the penult is counted over vowels.
new_statements.exceptions: Under (d), in languages that merged prenasalised stops with voiced stops a preceding vowel may be compensatorily lengthened (cited contrast: Rahambuu kombera vs Kodeoha ko:bera 'machete'), and a 'prestress' lengthened vowel may reflect an intermediate pronunciation; neither is an exception to penultimate placement.

audit.reasoning: Quote check: both deciding quotations (Mead 1998:97 sec. 3.1.2; Mead 1999:101 note (g)) are present verbatim in the copies we hold at the stated locators. The classification (penultimate, fixed) rests on a family-level blanket statement in a 1998 comparative PhD by the sole fieldworker on Rahambuu plus a phonemicisation convention in his 1999 survey; no Rahambuu-specific description of any kind exists (Glottolog: 0 descriptive refs, Glottolog's most extensive description wordlist-or-less), so this is the best available and we hold it. While checking I scanned sec. 1.5 (printed p. 16) of the same held dissertation and found a sharper statement the record did not cite: 'Stress is penultimate (non-phonemic), with suffixation usually precipitating stress movement.' This confirms the penultimate coding and refines the currently not stated by the source domain field (stress is computed over the suffixed word; 'usually' leaves room for some non-shift
